title: Granular batch-shed & KV prioritization with fallback-model orchestration
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem: Under certain high-concurrency tails we observe transient GPU memory pressure that leads to hard OOMs and full-request failures. Existing approaches (coarse eviction tiers and full-batch rejection) either cause poor request-level QoS or slow recovery. This ticket designs and implements a coordinated approach that 1) estimates per-request incremental memory weight at admission time, 2) performs granular batch shedding instead of blanket batch rejection, 3) reserves a compact KV slot pool for in-flight high-priority requests, and 4) orchestrates automated fallback to smaller/quantized model variants with transparent retries and telemetry. Goals: - Prevent hard OOMs by keeping a live safety buffer on each GPU. - Minimize user-visible failures by degrading quality (smaller/quantized model, truncated completion) rather than returning error. - Keep tail latency SLOs reasonable for P0/P1 requests while shedding best-effort work. - Provide observability and lineage for any automatic fallback/retry so downstream teams can decide to opt out.

Proposed design (high level):
- Memory-weight estimator: lightweight predictor runs at admission to predict incremental GPU memory needed for the request given model variant, sequence length, and current KV occupancy. Uses simple linear model with per-model coefficients (fast, CPU-bound). Output: mem_weight_bytes.
- Admission controller with multi-constraint packing: maintain per-GPU budgets: total_mem_active, reserved_kv_pool, safety_buffer. Admission decision steps:
  1) If mem_weight + active_mem > total_mem - safety_buffer => attempt graceful mitigation.
  2) Graceful mitigation order: per-request priority downgrade (reduce max_tokens or force shorter output), try smaller model variant (fallback chain), or attempt soft KV eviction from cold slots (see eviction policy). If mitigation succeeds, accept.
  3) If multiple requests queued, perform granular batch-drop: drop lowest-priority requests within the batch rather than entire batch; ensure minimum batch size to avoid throughput cliff.
- KV prioritization: mark KV entries with priority bands (hot, warm, cold). Reserve a small fraction (3-5%) of KV memory as 'reserved pool' for high-priority in-flight requests; eviction must avoid trimming reserved pool unless emergency.
- Soft eviction and speculative snapshotting: when evicting warm entries, create quick in-memory compressed snapshots (delta compaction) to allow faster rehydration for short-lived retries.
- Fallback-model orchestration: maintain per-customer fallback chains (e.g., rlarge->rmedium-quant->rsmall-int8). When fallback is used, attach metadata to response headers and to a persistent event in observability pipeline.
- Retry/backoff semantics: single automated retry on fallback success path with exponential backoff jitter. If fallback fails, return degraded response with explicit code and link to troubleshooting doc.
- Telemetry: add counters and histograms for mem_weight predictions vs actual, frequency of fallback, batch-shed rate, per-model fallback latencies, and customer impact tags.

Implementation plan (phases):
- Phase 0: Simulation harness: inject synthetic mem_weight signals and replay production traces to quantify benefits of granular-shed vs whole-batch reject. (owner: Marco)
- Phase 1: Lightweight mem predictor + admission hook + policy config flags behind feature gate. Add metrics. (owner: Marco)
- Phase 2: KV priority bands + reserved pool + soft snapshotting primitives. (owner: Storage team)
- Phase 3: Fallback chain orchestration + retry semantics + response metadata + audit events. (owner: Marco + Launch)
- Phase 4: Canary rollout on 1 rack, monitor for regressions, expand.

Constraints and trade-offs: 
- Mem predictor simplicity vs accuracy: we prefer biased-to-overestimate approach to avoid under-provisioning; may reduce throughput slightly.
- Dropping requests within batch increases head-of-line variability and complicates client-level correlation; mitigated via clear observability and client guidance.
- Snapshotting increases CPU and transient memory usage; tune snapshot size and eviction frequency.

acceptance_criteria: Simulated replay shows >70% reduction in hard OOMs in peak tail compared to baseline while keeping average throughput loss <10%
End-to-end canary on single rack shows <0.5% increase in P99 latency for P0 requests and <1% request error rate attributable to memory failures
Telemetry surfaces mem_weight prediction error histogram and fallback events with customer tags
Fallback chain succeeds for at least 95% of candidate cases and annotated response headers/audit events are emitted
Integration tests exist that exercise granular batch-shed and verify that low-priority requests are dropped before high-priority ones within a batch
rollout_plan: Feature gated rollout: enable simulation traffic -> internal beta on non-critical clusters -> single-rack canary (monitor 48h) -> gradual ramp 10/25/50/100%. Rollback: disable feature gate and flush reserved KV pool if regressions observed.
testing_plan: Unit tests for mem-weight estimator under synthetic distributions
Integration tests for admission controller with mocked total_mem pressure
Chaos tests: inject sudden KV eviction pressure and ensure fallback triggers without hard OOM
A/B experiment vs baseline to measure real customer impact metrics (error rate, latency, cost)
risks: Over-conservative mem estimates could reduce throughput and increase cost for customers
Incorrect priority tagging could cause high-priority requests to be shed; require conservative default mapping and opt-in overrides
Snapshotting CPU overhead may cause contention with model kernels on shared nodes; will monitor CPU steal and tune snapshot frequency
